seg_p0032_s0001: THE ANTIQUITIES OF THE BRITISH CHURCHES.
seg_p0032_s0002: CHAPTER I. The Britons idolaters before they received the Christian faith. Concerning the apostles who are said to have first preached the gospel in the British Isles: James the son of Zebedee, Simon the Zealot, Simon Peter, and the blessed Paul. Likewise concerning Aristobulus and Claudia the British woman.
seg_p0032_s0003: No one need doubt that, in those times of ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish underwent the common lot of the other nations — that is, that they were “without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers as regards the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” For, as the impious Porphyry once said, “neither had Britain, a province fertile in tyrants, nor the Scottish peoples and all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, known Moses and the prophets.” Nor are the learned men who maintain that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of one God any less mistaken than Postel was when he trifled in attempting to derive the origin of the Irish from the Hebrews. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, indicates plainly the contrary — that “the land of Britain, before the advent of Christ, by no means agreed in the religion of one God”; and specifically Dio Cassius has recorded that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons; and concerning their idol-madness their own countryman Gildas furnishes so clear a testimony that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: “Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, common to all the nations, by which the whole human race was bound fast before the advent of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of my country, almost exceeding in number those of Egypt, some of which we still behold, with their features yet misshapen, within or without the deserted walls, rigid after the usual manner with their grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once deadly but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, &c.” So that the blessed Jerome, in his epitaph of Nepotian, did not hesitate to pronounce upon the most wretched condition of those times and the most happy condition of those that followed: “Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the rigid region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — peoples so innumerable, and multitudes of nations so great; how varied in their tongues, how varied in the fashion of their dress and their arms?”
seg_p0032_fn_002: In Jerome, Letter to Ctesiphon, Against the Pelagians.
seg_p0032_fn_003: Camden, Britannia, pp. 47, 48, London edition of 1607. Fr. Godwin, On the Conversion of Britain, chapter 3, section 23 — in whom Origen is to be substituted for Tertullian.
